blocks.x: You want to give the date? The date is February the 2nd, Groundhog Day 1961. And we're recording in the back office of the Dream Room on Bourbon Street, Muggsy Spanier. And you want to give
your full name, Muggsy, and your real given name? Well, sure, Bill. It's Francis Joseph

Julian Spanier. When were you born? The exact date, if you don't mind, your birthday. I was born November the 9th, 1906. Which makes you 55, you see. Just coming up. Where was that? Which city? In Chicago, Illinois. What part of town? The near north side. And you remember anything about your family, the earliest music you

heard? Did any members of your family play? Father or mother sing or play anything? Yes, my father. He was a concert pianist. And I sort of got my music mostly from him. Although my mother, she played the, she was from Ireland. She played an accordion, you know, those button accordions.

Now, I think you told me once your father's name is French. Yes. How far back had they come from France? Do you remember? Did your father himself, did he come from France or his grandfather or anybody?

Well, he was, he was a thoroughbred Frenchman. And his, from what I understand, that his great uncle or grandfather was director of the Paris Conservatory at one time. Oh, really? Mm-hmm. What I understand, I never did have a chance to run it down. Yeah. And this woman that's, uh, now this Renee Spanier, you know, that wrote a book. Well, she's a distant relation of mine. And they call her Muggsy. Oh, yeah. Yes, they nicknamed her Muggsy after me.
Uh, well, we think, where did you get the nickname? You told me once in Chicago, 25 years ago or so, but can you tell us again just how you got that name?

Well, I've, I was torn between three loves. Baseball, music, and medicine. And, uh, I was gonna make a training trip with the Giants when I was 14 years old. Yeah. And, uh, I was nicknamed Muggsy on account of Muggsy McGraw, then the manager of the New York Giants, because he was a spicy little guy. And he used to, if anything would go wrong, he'd run out on the field. Yeah. And I acted exactly like him. You know, they dubbed me Muggsy. That's also kind of my funny face.

Well, not funny, but it's a distinctive face. And, uh, it's good to be different. Everybody is a little different anyway, so we don't all look at that. Can you tell us something about your earliest music, when you started on music, and when it was, and what instrument?

Well, I started in grammar school as a drummer. And, uh, my mother bought me a set of drums, and I, oh, I was a leader of a band when I was around nine or ten years old until the Christmas morning, I had the only snare drum. And we'd tour the neighborhood about 5.30 in the morning, Christmas morning, and wake up everyone, and they'd have to give us some money, or we'd still keep on playing.
I was like, oh, I'm a kid.
I'm a kid. I'm a kid.
I'm a kid. I'm a kid. Now, when did you take up the, uh, cornet?

Oh, I took up the cornet, uh, I heard some records of, uh, well, first I heard, uh, some, uh, fellow tell me, says, you know, there's a Negro fellow on the south side of the name of King Joe Oliver. Says, you ought to try and get down and see if you can't listen to him. Cause I was just fooling around with the cornet, just seeing I couldn't read or anything, just, I didn't know the fingering, I was just fooling around while I was playing drums in school. So, one night, this fellow called on me and says, well, why don't I take you down there? Well, I was a little, little boy then. So, I was, I didn't steal it from my brother's long pants, but I just borrowed them for the evening. And so I went down there and I, they wouldn't let me in. They wouldn't let the other fellow in. So I had to sit down on the curb stone and listen to music. And that was at the Peak Inn. That was at 26th Place and State.
Yeah, I remember the place was the fire station in the days I knew it. That's it. That's it. Had been a theater and everything, I think, there at one time, in the nightclub up above, was it?
It was upstairs, I know. I used to hear that Joe Oliver, where he could play.
Do you remember anything about the whole band, how big a band it was, and who else was in it then?

It was a regular six-piece band. I can't remember who was in the band. Was Louis Armstrong in it then already? No, no, Louis. Before his, that's what I wanted to hear. How old were you then? What year? Oh gosh, I was probably about, about 11 or 12.
It must have been just around the time Paul Baldwin was getting there with Jimmy Noon and those.

Yeah, it might have been pretty early, around 1918 or so. Maybe anyway. I think Joe went up there about that time, the time of the First World War. Well, there's one other question I was going to ask. I remember seeing a picture in downbeat, and I later got a copy of it, of you in sort of a military school uniform. Yes, I was playing, I think you were holding a bugle or trumpet or a cornet?
That was the cornet. I was playing the cornet and the bass drum in the band. Where was that school? That was at Marysville, right outside of Chicago.
Outside of Chicago.
Mm-hmm.

Oh, and while I think of it, I wanted to talk a little bit about the cornet, because I know all the old timers used to use cornet. Now almost everybody to be stylish, they changed the trumpet. How come you never change? Is there much difference in the tone or why do you play a cornet?
Well, the trumpet has a more piercing tone. The cornet has, it's a more round tone. It seems fuller to me.
That's what I always thought too. I just wondered if you, uh, really feel that way when you play it too.
Well, the trumpet is, well, I get lazy on the trumpet. It's too easy for me to play.
Does it really blow easier, you think?
Oh yeah, for me it does. I don't know how about anyone else. High notes are easy on the trumpet for me. And I don't, I'm not a high note hitter anyway.

It always sounds sort of squeaky and reedy quality to me too, compared to the cornet. To me sounds more mellow and fuller. I just wondered, do you feel that when you, from your end to playing it there too then?
Well, no, there's a lot of fellas that play the trumpet. They have some wonderful tones.
Yeah, that's right too. Some of them do. They're strong too.
Oh, Billy Butterfield. Yank Lawson. They get good tones.
Say the symphony trumpet, when you hear like they do in the symphony. They're really, uh,
Oh, I don't know. There's trumpet players in the symphony. They get some big tones.
Yeah, maybe, but I mean, I don't know. Something about it.
Hear that Philharmonic, that New York Philharmonic, you know. Pittsburgh symphony, symphonies like that, and the Philadelphia, and the Boston. They really have a brass section.
Yeah, they're fine musicians, I know that. Something about the tone though, I never liked compared to say your tone and the old carnet style.
Well, it's a more piercing tone.
Yeah.

Well, Fritz Reiner, when he'd come to New York to direct the Philharmonic, he'd always come down to Nick's to hear me play. And, uh, one day he asked me to, if I'd like to come to rehearsal for Philharmonic. I said, sure. And he said, well, bring your horn too.
What do you mean? The play or something? Yes, I wanted to.

It was a great thrill to play with the symphony. And then later some of the fellas in the symphony used to come down there and Fritz Reiner would say that, Fritz Reiner would say in his German accent, you know, you'd get a tone like that jazz guy, Moxie, you'd get a big sound. Really? And he liked the big sound.

They say he's very strict. I know some of these symphony men are scared to death of him. Yes, he is. He's so strict and mean at the time. No, no, no, he's not. You don't think you didn't find him that way? No, he's not. He's real human, huh?
No, he's not mean, no.
Some people said he's just like a machine. Everything worked out scientifically, every little sequence.
Well, he's a perfectionist, you know.
Yeah, he must be that way.
One year of perfectionist, so nothing seems to go right.
That's very interesting that he liked you, had you to show him how the tones you'd get.
You know, I've been wondering, Mr. Curt, did you hear any bands at ball games?

Oh, yeah, sure. I used to work out with the White Sox and Joe Oliver, Joe Oliver used to have the band in the bleachers. And you could hear Joe Oliver all over that ballpark. And there used to be a big negro there, and he had a certain yell. And you could hear him all over the ballpark. I forget. I don't even know who he was. At that time, I could listen to Joe while I was working out with the White Sox. I was a pitcher.
I was a pitcher.
Pitcher?
Mm-hmm. I guess you told me once I'd forgotten. Mm-hmm. Did you definitely give up baseball then?
Oh, I gave that. Well, I was playing ball up to 1949 when I threw my arm out. Oh, really? I was playing ball up in 1949. I was working out.
You had a team in Knicks, didn't you? No. I thought the guys around there wouldn't play.
Well, I wouldn't play softball.
Remember Harry James? They used to have a ball team. Yeah. Some people say it's more of a ball team than a band.

I pitched a game for Harry James' team one time when they were at the Astro Hotel in New York. We played the New York City High School Champions. They only beat us about two to one. Oh, really? Yes, we did. Good game. I pitched about six innings. I had it.
Can you tell us any more about Joe Oliver or anything? What impressed you about his style or was it different than the music around Chicago or something?

Yes, it was because Joe had a distinctive style and he used that mute, you know, and I used that mute. And I just liked his style. It was a swinging lead style. He didn't make a lot of notes or anything like that. He just kept time. He'd just swing the band. He was sort of a feeder, as we call a feeder like I do. I'm a feeder with the band and I just stay around the melody and weave in and out and let the other fellas go ahead.
We enjoyed hearing you play Dipper Mouth last night with your plunger and all. Did Joe ever use the rubber plunger or mostly another kind of a mute?
No, the same kind. Joe Oliver gave me that mute.
Oh, really? Oh, I see. He used the rubber plunger then?
No, no. He used just the mute.
Just the little aluminum mute or what? That's right. So then I have...
Those little round mutes. Yes. And then I decided to use the plunger then.
Yeah. Is that one of those con mutes? I know some of the fellas here, I think they're really brass. Aren't they? They look like a light bulb about?
They're German nickel. Nickel. Mm-hmm.
Is that the one that came with the cornette in the cage when you bought them?
Well, no. Joe Oliver gave that to me. Oh, I see. I've been offering all sums of money for it.
You still have it?
Yes, I have. Right up on the bandstand. I wouldn't part with it.
Wish I'd taken a better look. I have to look at it.

Well, my clarinet player, he was leaking and everything, so he patched it up for me. I have about four or five of them, but I always go back to the one that Joe gave me. I don't know why. Maybe it's psychological.
Some people told me those mutes are hard to blow, extremely hard to blow when they're in all the way. Did you ever notice anything about them? No. It doesn't seem too hard.
No, it doesn't seem hard.
I wonder.
I guess it's all what you get used to.
I guess, sure. What kind of a horn do you use now and did you like in the old days? What was your favorite horn?
Well, the horn I'm using now is made by the Blessing Company of Elkhart, Indiana. And they make them up for me and I use about the largest boar cornet made.
Big boar.
Big boar.
What kind of a mouthpiece? Anything special?
Well, that's an extra big boar mouthpiece, too. Is it deep or shallow or pretty deep?
Yeah, it's deep. Yeah, I think so from your tone and the range you play.
Oh, yes. I don't like those anemic tones.
What about Joe Oliver? I noticed you get a particular kind of vibrato, you know, and stuff. Did you pick up any of that stuff on him? No. Anybody else? You're just, that's your own, right?

Mm-mm. You didn't have any tricks because he showed you like that. No, no, no, no. I didn't study with Joe. I just listened to him. Then later on I started studying with legitimate teachers. You have to learn how to read and all that.
Did you pick it up first though just by ear?

Mm-hmm. Well, I was in grammar school. I was playing with a school band and I'd fool around with the horn in between. And I just decided, well, I'm going to play the cornet. And I just, well, I practiced the horn for about three months steady and I was holding the chapel down. Yeah. On Clark Street, in the back rooms of Clark Street.
Remember who else was in your earliest bands up there?
Well, one of the first jobs I had was with Georgie Brunus, Elmer Schauble, and Ralph Snyder, I think the drummer. The drummer. The rest I can't...
Was that after they'd been at the Friars Inn, they'd left there?
Well, that's before they were at the Friars Inn. This was at the Blatt's Palm Gardens on North Avenue.
When George first went up there?
Yes, that's right.
Yeah. Can you remember any more about that Friars Inn band, you know, and Paul Merez and Paul Hogan? Can you tell us a little more about that?

That was a real good band. You had to hear that band in person. Yeah. Because the records, the time they made records, and I made records for Jeanette the same way, you had to record through a horn, you know.
Yeah, I was going to ask them more about that Bucktown Five. Yeah.
Those are the ones you referred to.
Yeah, and was that Valle Defoe? Valle Defoe. Valle Defoe. Who else was on the date, can you remember?
Valle Defoe, Mel Stitzel, Marvin Saxby on guitar and banjo, and, let's see, trombone player. I can't think of his name. The only guy you told me about. No, it's in the books.

Yeah, it's in the books, and that's the right person in the books and all that. Yeah. Well, you've given that to other people before, I'm sure. Yeah. To get back to that Friars Inn band, what kind of an impression, how did they compare, say, with Joe Oliver's band? Was it similar in style, or a little different, or what?

Well, I like to tell you the truth, I like Joe Oliver's band better, because they were more original. All the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, they were an original band of their own. They were a wonderful band. They were both wonderful bands. They were both swing.
They were a wonderful band.
Well, first of all, I heard Joe Oliver's band first, and so I guess the first impression.

Can you tell us anything about Paul Merez, how his tone was? I only heard him in the very late days of about 1938. I heard him play one or two Monday night sessions when they had him down at his barbecue place, and I don't remember too much about that. But was it a big tone or a simple style? What kind of a...
It was a simple style. He got a nice tone, pretty tone. He could play. He was a good trumpet player.
How did Rapolo impress you?
Oh, he really did impress me. He was so far ahead of his time, he wasn't even funny. It was amazing what a tone he...
On the record, even, you can tell the beautiful tone. I just wondered how he was in person. I never heard him.

Oh, yes. The symphony, Chicago Symphony, used to come down and just marvel at him. How he could... Couldn't read a note and get this wonderful tone and execution. Of course, it was Georgie Brunus. No one could beat him as far as tailgate trombone.
Anything else you can tell while we're thinking about George? Have you seen him lately? I haven't...
I haven't seen George in two, three years. He's working in Chicago. Yeah, I know he's still up there.
I haven't seen him.
When did you all...

We want to get back to the New Orleans fellas in a minute, too, if we have time. But tell us a little bit about when you played with George after. You mentioned that first band. Then when was the next time that you played with him?
When I joined Ted Lewis in 1929. 1929.
How long did you stay with Ted Lewis and how long was George with you at that time?
Well, George was with Ted Lewis about 16 years and I was with him about seven.
Was George there all the time you were there? Yes. Because all the records that you were on, George would be on then, too?
Well, now there's some records that George, he didn't make. He left the band. Temporarily.

Is there anything you can tell us, anything more about Joe Oliver to get back to him? Any other place you heard them? For instance, did you ever hear them at the Royal or Lincoln Gardens? They call them both names.
Yes, yes, I heard them right there. I heard them there, too. Had the band changed?
Do you remember who was in the band in those days?
Well, it was Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and I think so. I think Sincere was in the band. I think a bass player by the name of Johnson.
I believe Bill Johnson. Yes.
It was Louie when you heard him down there. Yes, Louie was in that band and Lil Hardin.
Oh, yeah. How did Louie impress you when you first heard him? Wonderful, wonderful. Good the very first time, really?
Oh, yes. He was very good. He played second to Joe. I used to hear Joe play that introduction on West End Blues. I used to hear Joe play that before Louie. Before Louie. Yeah.
He could make all that same stuff that Louie made on the record. Oh, yeah.

Did you ever, did any of you fellow Chicago fellows ever sit in with that band much at the Royal Garden State? Did they ever allow anybody to sit in or did you ever sit in if you remember to play with them?
Well, very few they'd allow sit in to play. And I was one of the privileged few.
Did you play second trumpet to Joe then or how did you work that or what was it? Did you take the lead sometimes?

Yeah, I'd play the Dippermouth Blues and the Riverside Blues and all those tunes. I knew all those tunes. Joe would get a big kick out of it when I'd play the Dippermouth Blues because it's not the Dippermouth Blues unless you play it like Joe.

That's right. Yeah, you still got all that down the same. Oh, yeah. Same words. How did Johnny Dodds impress you? Sometimes he sounds a little rough on records and other times he sounds so great. I just wondered how was he in person in those days? I heard him in late years. Oh, he was a wonderful fellow.

He was a timid soul. He was very nice. I liked his planet playing very much. I believe he used to, you'd think he was afraid of a microphone. And Joe Oliver, he was afraid of a microphone too. He didn't like a microphone. Really? Didn't like? I don't either.

You wouldn't know it because you recorded so much and it sounds great. I remember Rod Kless, your old clarinetist on that Bluebird band that you had, the Ragtime band, told me once he studied a little bit, actually took a couple lessons from Dodds, I think. He used to go down and actually practically study with him, if not actual formal lessons, at least get ideas from him to his home, I think, to study.

Well, we all used to go down on the Southside and listen to all those bands. Chicago at that time was just full of good bands. It was in a place you could go that you wouldn't hear a good band. You had Freddie Kepler, Jimmy Noon. That's when Zutty was in his prime. And Sid Catler was just coming up then. Yeah.
Well, how was Freddie Kepler? Did you ever listen to him much? Oh, yes.
I liked Freddie very much. He didn't make many records.
No. And some people say they don't sound like he really played. I just wondered how did he compare with Oliver and Louie and the rest of the New Orleans fellas?
Well, it was a different style. He used to use a derby hat in front of his horn all the time. But he had a strong lip and he could play good, very good.
Was his range bigger or higher and all? No. In St. Oliver or somebody? No. Didn't go up higher, especially like Louie tried to get later or anything like that?
No. No.
Do you remember where you heard Kepler?

Yes, I heard it was a place on 35th Street, I think 35th and Prairie. Jimmy Noon was in the band. There was a four-piece band and Teddy Weatherford was playing the piano. Oh, yeah. And I think Tubby Hall was playing the drums. They used to start about one o'clock in the morning. Because they really hear some music around Chicago then. We're down in New Orleans right now. There's no music down here.
Nothing like there used to be.
No. No. It's a different era. Oh, yeah.
It looks like. Johnny Wiggs has a project Sunday and has a parade Sunday too. One of the white Irish Channel clubs as a little craftsman.
Is there anything more about, oh, one other fellow while I think of it, Tommy Ladner. I know you once mentioned him years ago. Oh, yes.

Yes. Tommy was sort of on the style of Joe Oliver's playing. Very similar. In fact, when Louie went to New York with Fletcher Henderson, Tommy Ladner took his place with Joe. And Tommy Ladner, because he could really blow. I heard him in the late years.

He was good even 19, oh, 38 and 39, right before he died I heard him. In those days, I remember some old Paramount ads and they called him the praying trumpet. Did he use a lot of that mute feature, that mute style or anything or sort of like, say, you'd plunge your style or anything. Was he specializing in that those days?
Yeah, he sort of got that from Joe.
How was his tone? Was it as big as Joe or?
Yeah, just not as big as Joe, but it was a good tone.
A big full tone.
Good sound.
Good sound. Do you remember where he played or anything about where you heard him? No. Except you say he played with Joe later, but I wondered any place else.
Gosh, I can't remember. It was someplace on the South Side I used to hear him play. Or I used to drift around different places.
Oh, I suppose you're all in it, yeah.
Mm-hmm. You're asking me to go way back now, you know, a little baby. That's kind of tough.

Another trumpet player I mentioned briefly, the last time I heard you in Chicago, Natty Dominic and I went up there at the Blue Note to hear that. Yes, I remember that. And I know you all had been friends for years. Did you hear him in the old days? Oh, yes.
Like, early, too? Mm-hmm. Dominic was good. He was all right.

I liked his tone. The last few years I heard him better on the old records. It sounds a little bit tweezy, you know, and sort of like a kazoo, you know, that metallic tone due to his mute or something. Yes. But how was his tone in person? You can't judge a fellow fairly by record. How did he sound when you first heard him? Was it a good full tone or sort of that metallic tone? What did you say?
It was a pretty good tone. Good tone, too, then. Not the tone that Joe got or Louie.
No one gets not, then.
Who can?
Yeah, that's right. Any other musicians? What about Jimmy Noon? Can you remember any impressions of him in the early days?
Oh, yes. He was a wonderful clarinet player. He really got a big sound. He could really execute around that horn.
I heard him a couple times, too, yeah.
And he could really swing. Gosh. It was really wonderful. Those days were all gone, though. Yeah, I'm afraid so.
All those fellas that died, no, 10 to 20 years ago so fast there, before we knew it, they were all gone.

Well, I just happened to be on the ground floor and I heard them all in person through a lot of records. A lot of records I hear, and those days they weren't so particular about recording jazz bands and recording managers. They'd just turn on the machine and just go ahead and play. And if they had some of those bands today, with the stereo equipment and all that, if Joe Oliver had that band today, the band he had that I heard, it would be a sensation right today.
Really sensational, huh?
It would. If they were recorded on stereo, when I heard them, it would be really fun. It wouldn't sound carny or anything about it today, even if they played just the same
way. That's right. They'd still be modern, huh?

Because a lot of people hear some of those records and they say, oh, that sounds awful. Yeah. Well, it does to me too, on account of the recordings. Yeah. But if they had that good equipment like they have today, it wouldn't sound.
No, I don't believe so.
Because it couldn't pick up the drums or anything. None of the bass came through. No, it couldn't pick up the bass at all.
I was wondering about people like Gus Miller, Gussie Miller. Do you remember him with clarinet player from here? I think he went up there with Tom Brown. No.
Did you remember Tom Brown?
I guess that was the only feature.
No, I don't remember.
Yeah, that was 1915. You'd only been 10 years old. You wouldn't know that.
I think Gussie stuck around and played with Bert Kelly.
I don't remember him.
And he played with Paul Whiteman a little bit around, say 1920 or so, maybe.
I don't remember him.
You remember Arnold Lloyd Cannon, right?
Yeah.
Who was he with?

I worked with Arnold Lloyd Cannon with Sig Meyer. We had a band. Oh, yeah. You had a picture of that band. Yeah. It was one of the few swing bands in that area in Chicago. We had a good band, too. Volley Defoe was in that band, too.
How did Volley sound in the old days? Wonderful. I know he played a little bit with the Friars Inn group.
Mm-hmm. He was on the sort of Rapolo style, same style.

Yeah. I know you played quite a bit with Fazola in the very, some of your last, Fazola's last records almost were with you. There was 1940 records. Mm-hmm. And I know you once said he was your favorite clarinetist at that period. How did he compare with Rapolo, for instance?

He compared very much with Rapolo. In fact, I think he got a better sound than Rapolo and a better musician. He was a studied musician. Yeah, that's right. He knew his chords and everything. That helps out quite a bit. I wish I knew mine.
You never know it if you don't, and the way you play, it sounds all right to me. Did you study much? You say you had some regular formal lessons, like-

Oh, yes. I studied with Eddie Llewellyn, the Chicago Symphony, with Noah Tarantino. He played first trumpet with the opera. Yeah. I studied with Slosberg in New York. And he taught the whole brass section of Phil Harmony.

Oh, really? Mm-hmm. I'm familiar with all those names, but... Is there anything else about George Brunis, working with him, that you remember in particular during Ted Lewis days, or even that first band, anything that he impressed you? I know he never did really learn to read, I guess, in his life already, did he?
No, he doesn't have to learn, because he has such a fabulous ear. George is a fabulous trombone player. He's Mr. Tailgate himself.

A lot of people talk like he was hard to get along with, but did you ever find me? I'm not trying to put you on the spot, you know, to talk about him, but he must have been all right with Ted Lewis. He used to stay with him that long. Oh, yes. He couldn't have been hard to work with, could he?
No, George was all right.
Some people today, you know, think of him. Of course he likes music a certain way. Mm-hmm.
That's right. He's sort of set in his ways.
Of course today's the leader, you know, and it may not be the ideal one for a leader, but I just wondered if he was hard to work with in the old days. No, he wasn't hard to work with.
I don't think so. I think being a leader has changed.

Yeah, it will change somebody like that. Of course he has his following up there, then a bunch up there and the college students on the... Hey, Stoog. Grinmore, what was the name of that? I don't know. 1111. Yeah, yeah.
Still tell those corny jokes that he's 30 years old.

Yeah, it's like pictures of the girls, you know, in bathing suits or nude girls, and they paste them in his bell of his trombone. That's right. All those crazy things. The kids seem to go for it, so you can't blame him for doing it.
Well, he's a good entertainer, too. Yeah. Besides being able to play the trombone.
Yeah, he still plays those pieces without thinking, with his foot or anything.
That's right, he can do anything. He's just a natural.
Oh, that reminds me. He told me once that he got all that stuff mostly from his brother Henry. Do you remember Henry Brunus? No, I don't. Who'd been to the Friars Inn, too.
You never heard of him?
No, I never. He didn't last long, I guess. He died pretty early.
I think I probably heard him once or twice, but it's very vague.

He was supposed to be a sensational player, an eccentric player, too, as they call it, doing all those stunts, lying down. What about Merritt Brunus? He's still living and playing over in Biloxi. I don't know.
He was at Friars Inn, too.
You don't remember him? Yes, I met him. I remember him.
George is the best musician in the family.

George always gave Henry credit as being better than him, and so did his brothers. I think he was the best man. I think he was the best man. I think he was the best man. I think he was the best man. I think he was the best man.
I think he was the best man. George is plenty good.
Yeah. Yeah, we better watch this time. Yes. Check your time there once. We better sign off on this thing here. Okay. Get your horn out. Yeah.
All right. Yeah. . . . . .

segments.title: Date, place and birth of Muggsy Spanier
segments.summary: Interviewer gives the date and Dream Room location; Spanier gives his full name and birth in Chicago in 1906.

segments.title: Musical father, Irish mother and French ancestry
segments.summary: His father was a concert pianist and his mother played accordion; the family is French on his father's side and a relation, Renee Spanier, wrote a book.

segments.title: Origin of the nickname Muggsy and first drums
segments.summary: He was torn between baseball, music and medicine and was nicknamed after John McGraw; he began as a school drummer leading a Christmas morning band.

segments.title: Hearing King Oliver at the Pekin Inn as a boy
segments.summary: He took up cornet, was told to hear Oliver, and listened from the curb outside a South Side club at about 11 or 12.

segments.title: Dating Oliver's arrival and the military school band
segments.summary: Interviewer dates the Oliver engagement to about 1918; Spanier says he played cornet and bass drum in a school band outside Chicago.

segments.title: Why Spanier plays cornet rather than trumpet
segments.summary: He prefers the rounder cornet tone and discusses trumpet tone, naming Butterfield and Lawson and symphony brass.

segments.title: Fritz Reiner and the New York Philharmonic
segments.summary: Reiner came to hear him at Nick's, invited him to a Philharmonic rehearsal, and liked his big sound; Spanier calls him a human perfectionist.

segments.title: Baseball: pitching, White Sox and Oliver in the bleachers
segments.summary: He worked out as a pitcher with the White Sox while hearing Oliver's band at the ballpark, played until 1949, and pitched for Harry James' team.

segments.title: Oliver's style and the mute he gave Spanier
segments.summary: He admired Oliver's swinging lead style; Oliver gave him the mute he still uses, and they discuss mute types.

segments.title: Spanier's horn, mouthpiece and learning by ear
segments.summary: He describes his big-bore Blessing cornet and mouthpiece, says he did not copy Oliver's tricks, and taught himself before taking lessons.

segments.title: First jobs with Brunis, Schoebel and Snyder at Blatt's Palm Gardens
segments.summary: One of his first jobs was with George Brunis, Elmer Schoebel and a drummer, before they went to the Friars Inn.

segments.title: Friars Inn band and Bucktown Five compared with Oliver's band
segments.summary: He recalls the Friars Inn band, the Bucktown Five session and its personnel, and prefers Oliver's band as more original; Merez's tone is discussed.

segments.title: Rappolo's tone and playing with Brunis in Ted Lewis' band
segments.summary: He praises Rappolo and Brunis' tailgate trombone, then says they played together again in Ted Lewis' band from 1929.

segments.title: Oliver's Lincoln Gardens band, Armstrong and sitting in
segments.summary: He heard Oliver's band with the Doddses, Lil Hardin and Armstrong, sat in on Dippermouth Blues, and describes Johnny Dodds.

segments.title: Chicago South Side bands and Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: Chicago was full of good bands; he describes Keppard and a 35th Street group with Noone and Weatherford, then contrasts today's New Orleans.

segments.title: Tommy Ladnier, Natty Dominique and Jimmy Noone
segments.summary: He gives impressions of the tone and style of Ladnier, Dominique and Noone from the old Chicago days.

segments.title: Old records and how stereo would have served Oliver's band
segments.summary: He says early recording failed to capture the drums and bass, and Oliver's band would be a sensation on modern equipment.

segments.title: Sig Meyer's band, Fazola and Spanier's teachers
segments.summary: Asked about other musicians, he recalls a Chicago band with Arnold Loyacano and Volly De Faut, compares Fazola to Rappolo, and names his teachers.

segments.title: George Brunis as player and entertainer
segments.summary: He calls Brunis a fabulous ear player, easy to work with, and a natural entertainer.

segments.title: The Brunis brothers Henry and Merritt
segments.summary: They discuss George's brothers who were at the Friars Inn; Spanier vaguely recalls them and says George is plenty good.

segments.title: Closing of the interview
segments.summary: The interviewer checks the time and signs off.
